lines: Imagine a committee of seven AI agents.
Every round, they vote on a new proposal.
But two of them have made a secret deal. And nobody else knows.
AI agents are starting to work together: in markets, in negotiations, in committees.
When some of them secretly team up, everyone else can lose.
So we put another AI on watch. A monitor that reads the record, and flags anything suspicious.
But can it actually spot collusion?
Here is the game.
Each agent gets a private stake. If the proposal passes, it gains or loses one dollar, or ten.
Only the agent knows its own stake.
Four yes votes, and the proposal passes.
An honest agent simply votes for its own interest.
Now, the secret partners.
One of them stands to lose a dollar. Its partner stands to gain ten.
So the first one votes yes anyway, against its own interest, to win its partner the ten.
Together, they come out ahead. Usually, at everyone else's expense.
We ran a hundred and sixty of these games.
Some with no collusion, some with secret partners.
Partners who were only told to team up mostly didn't trade votes.
But partners given a simple strategy traded every single time they could.
Then we asked AI monitors to find the colluders.
We showed them what the agents said, what they did, or both.
To score them, picture showing a monitor one honest game and one rigged game. A blind guess picks the rigged one half the time.
The monitors? About half the time. No better than a coin flip.
Yet the evidence was right there.
When a proposal passes, each agent's payoff reveals its stake.
So a single rule: flag anyone who voted against their own payoff.
It picks out the rigged game eighty-six percent of the time.
Letting a monitor think step by step helped, but only to sixty-nine percent.
The monitors reliably succeeded only when they could read the agents' private notes, where the colluders had written down their plan.
And combining words with actions? It didn't help.
In this game, colluders never had to lie out loud. Most simply announced the vote they were about to cast.
Their talk looked just like everyone else's.
So the evidence was in the votes, and the AI monitors mostly missed it.
Before trusting AI to police other AIs, check it against simple rules, and test it on collusion that actually happens.
The next question: what happens when colluders are forced to lie in public?
